issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these two items directly contradict each other: being able to talk about the trauma very easily is inconsistent with losing the thread and being unable to finish when trying to explain it. Partial clarity could coexist with fragmented recall, but not with both easy verbal access and marked inability to narrate the event.

vignette: Rafael Hernandez had always been drawn to the wilderness, finding solace in its vast expanses and rhythms. As a park ranger, he spent his days patrolling the trails, ensuring that visitors respected the land and its creatures. But it was on one of these patrols, three years ago, that Rafael's life took a devastating turn. He stumbled upon a group of poachers, who tortured him for hours, leaving him with physical scars that would never fully heal. The memories of that day haunted Rafael, refusing to cohere into a linear narrative. Some moments were seared into his mind - the sound of his own screams, the smell of sweat and blood - while others remained shrouded in darkness. When he tried to recount the event to himself or others, he found himself losing the thread, unable to finish the story. Rafael couldn't shake the feeling that his body had been permanently damaged by what happened, that he was now more vulnerable than ever before. This sense of physical vulnerability fed into a growing distrust of others. Rafael became convinced that he couldn't rely on anyone - not even his colleagues or family members - to keep him safe. He began to rehearse conversations in his head before any interaction, trying to anticipate potential threats and prepare himself for the worst. This habit soon extended beyond social interactions; Rafael found himself repeatedly checking doors and windows, convinced that something bad was waiting just outside. The fear of being caught off guard became an all-consuming threat, one that Rafael's body seemed to react to even before his mind could process it. When he encountered unexpected delays or obstacles - a slow-moving hiker on the trail, a jammed lock on his truck - Rafael's heart would start racing, his senses on high alert. He was certain that something terrible was lurking just around the corner, waiting to strike. As time passed, Rafael's behaviors became more entrenched. He began avoiding driving or being a passenger in vehicles, fearing the loss of control and potential danger. His social life suffered as well; Rafael stopped attending ranger meetings and community events, unable to shake the feeling that others would judge him or take advantage of his vulnerability. The memories of the traumatic event continued to haunt Rafael, surfacing at unexpected moments and sending him spiraling into a cycle of fear and avoidance. He numbed his feelings as best he could, trying to create distance between himself and the world around him. But this only seemed to intensify the threat; Rafael's body remained on high alert, reacting to every perceived danger with a ferocity that left him exhausted. Despite his efforts to manage these symptoms, Rafael couldn't shake the fear that he was going crazy - that his reactions since the event were evidence of some deeper psychological fracture. It was this fear that finally brought him to seek help, three years after the traumatic event. As he sat in the therapist's office, Rafael knew that he had hit rock bottom; he could no longer continue living in a state of constant vigilance and dread. "I just want to be able to walk through the woods without feeling like I'm walking into a nightmare," Rafael said, his voice barely above a whisper. "I want to trust myself again - to know that I can handle whatever comes my way."
